riskClassification.metaDescription: EU AI Act four-tier risk classification with guided Annex III wizard.
riskClassification.title: Risk Classification
riskClassification.intro: Classify your AI systems using the EU AI Act four-tier risk framework. The guided wizard walks you through Annex III categories to determine the correct risk level, with full classification history for audit purposes.
riskClassification.tiersIntro: The EU AI Act defines four risk levels. Each level carries different compliance obligations, from outright prohibition to minimal transparency requirements.

unacceptable.description: AI systems that pose an unacceptable risk to safety or fundamental rights. These are prohibited under Art. 5.
unacceptable.examples: Social scoring, real-time biometric identification in public spaces, manipulation techniques.

high.description: AI systems listed in Annex III or used as safety components. Subject to full compliance requirements (Art. 6-51).
high.examples: Biometric identification, critical infrastructure, employment decisions, law enforcement.

limited.description: AI systems with specific transparency obligations. Users must be informed they are interacting with AI (Art. 50).
limited.examples: Chatbots, deepfake generators, emotion recognition systems.

minimal.description: AI systems posing minimal risk. No mandatory compliance requirements, though voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.
minimal.examples: Spam filters, AI-enabled video games, inventory management systems.

riskClassification.annexIntro: The classification wizard guides you through the Annex III high-risk categories. If your AI system falls into any of these areas, it is likely classified as High Risk.
riskClassification.historyIntro: Every classification change is versioned with a timestamp, the author, the previous and new risk levels, and a rationale. This provides a complete audit trail for regulators.

oversight.metaDescription: Approval gates, review scheduling, and decision logging for EU AI Act Art. 14 compliance.
oversight.title: Human Oversight
oversight.intro: Implement Art. 14 human oversight requirements for high-risk AI systems. Configure approval gates at key lifecycle stages, schedule periodic reviews, and maintain a complete decision log for regulators.
oversight.gateTypesIntro: Oversight gates are checkpoints that require human review and approval before an AI system can proceed. Each gate is linked to a specific AI system and assigned to a reviewer.

gateTypes.description: Required before an AI system moves from Testing to Deployed status. Ensures all compliance requirements are met.
Triggered after deployment to verify the system performs as expected in production. Monitors for unexpected behavior.
Scheduled at regular intervals (e.g., quarterly). Reviews ongoing performance, drift, and continued compliance.
Automatically requested when an AI incident is reported against the system. Requires review before continued operation.
Required when significant changes are made to the AI system (new model, different data sources, expanded scope).

oversight.decisionIntro: Every oversight decision is logged with the reviewer, timestamp, decision outcome, and rationale. This forms the Art. 14 audit trail required for high-risk AI systems.

approve.body: System is cleared to proceed. The reviewer confirms all requirements are satisfied.

reject.body: System is not cleared. The reviewer documents the reasons and required remediation steps.

incidents.title: AI Incidents
incidents.intro: Track AI-specific incidents from initial report through resolution. Manage response timelines, coordinate tasks, and handle Art. 73 authority notifications for serious incidents involving high-risk AI systems.
incidents.typesIntro: AI SENTINEL tracks incident types specific to AI systems, distinct from data protection incidents handled in DPO Central.
incidents.lifecycleIntro: Every incident follows a structured workflow. Status transitions and timestamps are tracked for compliance evidence.
incidents.severityIntro: Severity levels prioritize response efforts and determine notification requirements.

low.description: Minor incident, limited impact. No regulatory notification required.

medium.description: Moderate impact, contained quickly. Internal review recommended.

high.description: Significant impact. Likely requires authority notification under Art. 73.

critical.description: Large-scale failure or safety risk. Immediate Art. 73 notification required.

incidents.art73Intro: Under EU AI Act Article 73, providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to the relevant market surveillance authority. AI SENTINEL tracks notification deadlines, recipient authorities, and submission status.

art73.whenBody: Serious incidents involving death, serious damage to health, property, or the environment, or serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure.
art73.timelineBody: Report immediately after establishing a causal link (or its reasonable likelihood) and no later than 15 days after awareness: 10 days if the incident involves a death, 2 days for widespread infringements or serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure. The system tracks elapsed time from the incident report date.
art73.includeBody: Description of the incident, affected AI system, severity, root cause analysis (if available), and corrective measures taken or planned.

incidents.timelineIntro: Each incident maintains a detailed timeline recording all events, status changes, task assignments, and communications.

transparency.metaDescription: Track EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligations per AI system: AI interaction disclosure, synthetic-content marking, emotion recognition, and deepfake labelling.
transparency.title: Transparency (Art. 50)
transparency.intro: Article 50 of the EU AI Act imposes transparency duties that cut across risk tiers: even a minimal-risk chatbot owes a disclosure. AI SENTINEL tracks the four Art. 50 obligations per AI system, splits them by who actually owes them, and counts down the one deadline that has a transitional period.
transparency.applicabilityBody1: Art. 50 has applied since 2 August 2026 (Art. 113). Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI, OJ L of 24 July 2026) grants systems placed on the market before that date a transitional period for the machine-readable marking duty in Art. 50(2), running to 2 December 2026.
transparency.applicabilityBody2: That grace period is the reason the AI Registry asks whether a system was placed on the market before 2 August 2026. Answer it accurately: it is the only input that moves the marking deadline, and the dashboard's “marking overdue” counter is derived from it.
transparency.obligationsIntro: Two are owed by the provider and two by the deployer. A single organization often holds both roles, but recording them separately is what lets you answer a regulator asking which hat you were wearing.

obligations.title: AI interaction disclosure
obligations.description: Systems that interact directly with people must make clear they are AI, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person. Chatbots and voice agents are the typical case.

obligations.title: Machine-readable marking of synthetic content
obligations.description: Systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text must mark their output in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated. This is the obligation with a transitional deadline: see below.

obligations.title: Emotion recognition and biometric categorisation
obligations.description: Deployers must inform the people exposed to an emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation system that it is in use. Note that several such uses are prohibited outright under Art. 5: the module flags that overlap rather than letting you record a disclosure for a practice you cannot lawfully run.

obligations.title: Deepfake and public-interest text labelling
obligations.description: Deployers publishing deepfakes must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The same applies to AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.

statuses.name: Not applicable
statuses.description: This obligation does not apply to the system. The default for every obligation until you decide otherwise.

statuses.name: Required
statuses.description: The obligation applies and is not yet satisfied. Systems in this state drive the deadline counters on the executive dashboard.

statuses.name: Implemented
statuses.description: The obligation applies and the disclosure or marking is in place. Record how in the AI statement so the evidence survives staff turnover.

workingSteps.body: Every AI system in the registry has a Transparency (Art. 50) tab alongside Models, Data Sources, and Risk Classification.
The module screens the system's purpose and technique and suggests which of the four obligations look applicable. Treat these as prompts, not conclusions: you confirm each one.
Mark each as Not applicable, Required, or Implemented. Anything left Required appears in the dashboard's transparency counters.
Record the disclosure wording and the marking method you actually use. This is the artifact a market surveillance authority will ask for; a status field alone will not satisfy them.

transparency.scopeBody: This module records your Art. 50 position; it does not mark content for you. Machine-readable marking is implemented in the generating system itself. AI SENTINEL is where you document which systems owe the duty, whether it is satisfied, and how: so the answer exists before someone asks for it.

compliance.metaDescription: Framework mapping for EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001 with evidence management and export.
compliance.title: Compliance
compliance.intro: Map your AI systems against leading regulatory frameworks. Track compliance status at the requirement level, attach evidence, and export compliance packages for regulators and auditors.
compliance.frameworksIntro: AI SENTINEL ships with eight pre-loaded frameworks: three that apply by risk tier (the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001) and five that apply by jurisdiction (the GDPR and the California, Colorado, Texas and Washington AI rules). Each framework is broken down into articles, clauses or functions with individual compliance tracking.

euAiAct.name: EU AI Act
euAiAct.description: Key-obligation mapping from Art. 4 (AI literacy) and Art. 5 (prohibited practices) through Art. 73 (serious incidents) and the Art. 113 applicability timeline, plus relevant annexes. The primary regulatory framework for AI systems in the European Union.

nist.name: NIST AI RMF
nist.description: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework. Four core functions with sub-categories.

iso.name: ISO 42001
iso.description: International standard for AI Management Systems. Covers organizational context, leadership, planning, support, and operations.

compliance.statusesIntro: Each requirement can be independently assessed for every AI system. The status reflects the current compliance posture for that specific requirement.
compliance.matrixIntro: The compliance matrix provides a per-AI-system view of all requirements within a chosen framework. For each requirement, you can set the compliance status, add notes, and attach evidence documents.
compliance.crossIntro: Many requirements across the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001 overlap conceptually. AI SENTINEL includes 41 pre-built cross-framework mappings so that one compliance effort can satisfy requirements across multiple frameworks simultaneously.
compliance.crossBody1: When you mark a requirement as <s>Compliant</s> or <s>Partially Compliant</s>, AI SENTINEL shows linked requirements from other frameworks and offers to propagate the status automatically.
compliance.crossBody2: For example, marking EU AI Act Art. 9 (Risk Management) as compliant can automatically update NIST GOVERN 1 (Risk Management Policies) and ISO 42001 Clause 6.1 (Actions to Address Risks): because they cover the same obligation.
compliance.snapshotBody1: When you classify an AI system's risk level (e.g., high risk under the EU AI Act), AI SENTINEL automatically creates compliance mapping records for every applicable requirement of the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001. The GDPR and the US state rules attach once the organization's jurisdictions and screening questions are answered. You arrive at the compliance matrix with the relevant controls pre-populated: no manual setup needed.
compliance.snapshotBody2: For a High Risk system, this means 80+ requirements are instantly initialized across EU AI Act (Art. 6 through Art. 73 key requirements), NIST AI RMF (all 23 practices), and ISO 42001 clauses, each set to “Not Assessed” and ready for evaluation.

shadowAi.metaTitle: Shadow AI Discovery: AI SENTINEL Docs
shadowAi.metaDescription: Discover unauthorized AI tools in your organization. Self-reporting portal, triage workflow, and promotion to formal governance.
shadowAi.title: Shadow AI Discovery
shadowAi.intro: Shadow AI refers to AI tools adopted by employees without the knowledge or approval of the organization. Research suggests that around 60% of employees use unapproved AI tools at work: from ChatGPT and Copilot to image generators and AI-powered analytics. Organizations cannot govern AI systems they do not know about.
shadowAi.whatP1: Shadow AI is the AI equivalent of Shadow IT: the use of AI-powered tools, services, and applications by employees without explicit organizational authorization. Unlike formally procured vendors that go through risk assessment and contract review, shadow AI tools enter the organization through individual adoption: an engineer installs a code assistant, a lawyer uses ChatGPT for contract review, a marketing team signs up for an AI copywriting tool.
shadowAi.whatP2: Under the EU AI Act, organizations that deploy AI systems have specific obligations as deployers: regardless of whether the deployment was sanctioned or not. Shadow AI creates blind spots in compliance, data protection, and risk management programs.

whyItems.title: Compliance risk
whyItems.description: Unregistered AI systems may fall under high-risk categories without appropriate conformity assessments, human oversight, or risk documentation.

whyItems.title: Data protection
whyItems.description: Employees may input personal data, trade secrets, or client information into AI tools that train on user inputs or store data in non-compliant jurisdictions.

whyItems.title: Regulatory exposure
whyItems.description: Under the EU AI Act, deployers are responsible for AI systems used within their organization: even those adopted informally by staff.

whyItems.title: Governance gap
whyItems.description: You cannot classify risk, run assessments, or set oversight gates for AI systems you do not know exist. Shadow AI is the missing first step.

shadowAi.vsIntro: Shadow AI Discovery and Vendor Risk Management solve fundamentally different problems in opposite directions. They are complementary, not overlapping.

Known from day one: the org chose the vendor
Core question: “Is this vendor we selected risky?”

howSteps.title: Approve or prohibit
howSteps.description: Each tool is either APPROVED for continued use (with conditions) or PROHIBITED and flagged for removal. Prohibited tools trigger a clear organizational signal that the tool is not sanctioned.

howSteps.title: Promote to formal governance
howSteps.description: Approved shadow tools can be promoted into the AI Registry as a formal AI System (and optionally into a Vendor record) in a single step. This bridges informal discovery into your full governance program.

whyItems.title: Due diligence at scale
whyItems.description: Manually researching each AI vendor's data practices, certifications, and risk posture is impractical. The catalog provides a standardized baseline for every vendor evaluation.

conformity.metaDescription: EU AI Act Art. 43 conformity assessment template for high-risk AI systems. Structured evaluation of technical documentation, quality management, and post-market monitoring.
conformity.title: Conformity Assessment
conformity.intro: High-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act must undergo a conformity assessment before being placed on the market. AI SENTINEL provides a structured template that walks your team through every requirement (from technical documentation to post-market monitoring) so nothing falls through the cracks.
conformity.whatP1: A conformity assessment is a formal evaluation process required by Art. 43 of the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems. It verifies that the AI system meets all applicable requirements before deployment: covering data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity.
conformity.whatP2: Depending on the use case, conformity assessments may be conducted internally by the provider or through a third-party notified body. In either case, the assessment must follow a structured methodology and produce documented evidence of compliance.

whoItems.title: AI Providers
whoItems.description: Organizations that develop or place high-risk AI systems on the EU market must complete a conformity assessment before deployment (Art. 16).

whoItems.title: AI Deployers
whoItems.description: Organizations deploying high-risk AI systems must verify that the provider has completed the conformity assessment and that the CE marking is in place (Art. 26).

whoItems.title: Annex III systems
whoItems.description: AI systems used in biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or administration of justice (Art. 6(2)).

whoItems.title: Internal compliance teams
whoItems.description: Even when a notified body is involved, internal teams need a structured process to prepare documentation, gather evidence, and track remediation of gaps.

coversItems.description: Verification that a risk management system is established and maintained throughout the AI system lifecycle (Art. 9).
Assessment of training, validation, and testing data: including relevance, representativeness, and bias examination (Art. 10).
Review of technical documentation completeness: system description, design specifications, development process, and performance metrics (Art. 11, Annex IV).
Evaluation of automatic logging capabilities for traceability, including input/output records and system events (Art. 12).
Assessment of instructions for use, disclosure of AI nature, and interpretability measures for deployers and affected persons (Art. 13).
Verification that appropriate human oversight measures are designed into the system and documented (Art. 14).
Testing and validation of accuracy levels, resilience to errors and adversarial attacks, and cybersecurity measures (Art. 15).
Review of the provider's quality management system covering development processes, testing, and post-market obligations (Art. 17).
Verification that a post-market monitoring plan is in place to detect and address issues after deployment (Art. 72).

howSteps.title: Work through each section
howSteps.description: Each section presents structured questions aligned to the EU AI Act requirements. Record findings, attach evidence, and note any gaps.

howSteps.title: Submit for review
howSteps.description: Once complete, submit the assessment for review by the AI Officer or governance lead. The approval workflow tracks sign-off and any requested changes.

howSteps.title: Document and maintain
howSteps.description: The completed assessment becomes part of your compliance record. Link it to the AI system's compliance mapping and revisit it when material changes occur.

biasFairness.metaDescription: Structured bias and fairness evaluation for AI systems. Detect discrimination risks, assess protected attributes, and document mitigation measures.
biasFairness.title: Bias & Fairness Assessment
biasFairness.intro: AI systems can produce discriminatory outcomes: often unintentionally. The Bias & Fairness Assessment provides a structured methodology to evaluate your AI systems for bias risks, document affected protected attributes, and track mitigation measures.
biasFairness.whatTitle: What is a Bias & Fairness Assessment?
biasFairness.whatP1: A bias and fairness assessment is a systematic evaluation of an AI system's potential to produce outcomes that unfairly disadvantage individuals or groups based on protected characteristics: such as race, gender, age, disability, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status.
biasFairness.whatP2: Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI systems must examine training data for possible biases (Art. 10) and implement measures to prevent discriminatory outcomes. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (Art. 21) explicitly prohibits discrimination, and AI systems that score, rank, or make decisions about people are particularly exposed to this risk.

whyItems.title: Legal obligation
whyItems.description: The EU AI Act requires bias examination of training data (Art. 10(2)(f)) and non-discrimination safeguards for high-risk systems. Failure to comply carries fines up to 3% of global turnover.

whyItems.title: Fundamental rights
whyItems.description: AI-driven discrimination can violate the right to non-discrimination (EU Charter Art. 21), equal treatment directives, and national equality legislation.

whyItems.title: Real-world impact
whyItems.description: Biased AI in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare triage, or law enforcement has documented consequences: rejected applicants, denied loans, missed diagnoses, and wrongful arrests.

whyItems.title: Reputational risk
whyItems.description: Public disclosure of biased AI outcomes causes lasting reputational damage. Proactive assessment demonstrates responsible AI governance to regulators, customers, and the public.

typesItems.description: Historical data reflects past discrimination. A hiring model trained on historical decisions inherits biases in who was previously hired or promoted.
The training dataset does not represent the population the system will serve. Underrepresented groups receive less accurate predictions.
The features or labels used as proxies are themselves biased. Using zip codes as a feature can encode racial segregation patterns.
A single model is applied to groups with different underlying distributions. Medical AI trained primarily on one demographic may underperform for others.
The system is used in a context different from the one it was designed for, or its outputs are interpreted in a biased manner by human operators.

coversItems.description: Identification of which protected characteristics (age, gender, race, disability, etc.) are relevant to the AI system's domain and affected population.
Evaluation of whether training and testing data adequately represents all relevant groups, including historically underrepresented populations.
Selection and application of appropriate fairness metrics: demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity, or individual fairness measures.
Analysis of whether ostensibly neutral features (location, language, education) serve as proxies for protected attributes.
Documentation of pre-processing, in-processing, or post-processing techniques used to reduce identified bias.
Ongoing monitoring strategy to detect bias drift after deployment, including thresholds and escalation procedures.

howSteps.title: Create a new assessment
howSteps.description: Select the Bias & Fairness template and link it to a registered AI system. The template structures the evaluation around the system's specific use case and affected population.

howSteps.title: Evaluate each dimension
howSteps.description: Work through the structured sections: identify relevant protected attributes, assess data representativeness, apply fairness metrics, and check for proxy variables.

howSteps.title: Document findings and mitigations
howSteps.description: Record identified bias risks with severity ratings. For each risk, document the mitigation approach: whether technical (algorithmic debiasing) or procedural (human review).

howSteps.title: Review and monitor
howSteps.description: Submit for approval, then establish ongoing monitoring. The assessment links to your AI system's record so bias findings inform risk classification and oversight decisions.

security.intro: AI SENTINEL is built for organizations that manage sensitive AI governance data. Security is embedded in every layer of the platform: from how we isolate your data to how we control access and protect your information.

isolation.title: Data Isolation
isolation.intro: Every organization on AI SENTINEL operates in a fully isolated environment. Your AI systems, assessments, policies, incidents, and vendor data are never accessible to other organizations.

items.title: Organization-Scoped Queries
items.description: Every database query is automatically scoped to your organization. There is no way to access another organization's data through the application.

items.title: Verified Membership
items.description: Before any operation, we verify that the requesting user is an active member of the organization. Membership is checked on every single request.

items.title: Cross-Tenant Protection
items.description: Operations that reference related entities (e.g., linking a policy to an AI system) verify that both entities belong to your organization.

items.title: Shared Reference Data Only
items.description: Only non-sensitive reference data (compliance frameworks, assessment templates) is shared across organizations. Your governance data is never shared.

accessControl.title: Access Control
accessControl.intro: AI SENTINEL enforces role-based access control (RBAC) across the entire platform. Every action is checked against your role before it is executed.
accessControl.readOnlyBody: Viewers have guaranteed read-only access. All write operations are blocked at the server level, not just the UI: preventing unauthorized modifications even through API calls.
accessControl.elevatedBody: Sensitive operations like approving assessments, publishing policies, and making oversight decisions require AI Officer, Admin, or Owner roles.

crossBorder.metaTitle: Cross-border AI governance: one assessment, six regimes | AI SENTINEL
crossBorder.metaDescription: Answer the EU AI Act, the GDPR, California ADMT, Colorado, Texas and Washington from a single impact assessment, and generate the notice and appeal protocol that follow.
crossBorder.title: Cross-border regimes
crossBorder.intro: Most organisations deploying AI answer to several regulators at once, and each asks a version of the same question in different words. AI SENTINEL resolves which regimes reach each system, asks one question set drafted to the strictest of them, and generates the documents each regime expects.
crossBorder.architectureBody1: The assessment has a common core that is always asked. Each core question is drafted to the strictest formulation among the regimes, so answering it once satisfies every regime that asks a weaker version of the same thing.
crossBorder.architectureBody2: On top of that core sit jurisdictional overlays. An overlay question appears only when that regime's rules have put the system in scope, so a European deployer is never asked about Washington health carriers, and a Texas-only business never sees a California section number.
crossBorder.architectureBody3: Every question declares which requirement codes its answer evidences. That is what lets one answer stand as evidence in several compliance registers at the same time, and it is what the generated documents cite.

regimes.name: EU AI Act
regimes.detail: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Risk classification, Annex III screening, the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment, Article 50 transparency, Annex IV technical documentation and the obligation calendar.

regimes.name: GDPR
regimes.detail: The AI-relevant articles, with Article 22 on solely automated decisions and Article 35 on impact assessments in full, including the CJEU reading that an automatically generated score can itself be the decision.

regimes.name: California CCPA ADMT
regimes.detail: The OAL-approved regulations: the three-prong human-involvement test, significant-decision domains, pre-use notice, opt-out, access, and the risk-assessment regime that has been live since January 2026.

regimes.name: Colorado SB 26-189
regimes.detail: The replacement statute that repealed the original Colorado AI Act. Advance notice, post-decision disclosure, correction and review, and developer documentation. Effective 1 January 2027, subject to pending federal litigation.

regimes.name: Texas TRAIGA
regimes.detail: House Bill 149, in force since January 2026. Intent-based prohibitions, government and health care disclosure duties, the NIST safe harbour and the regulatory sandbox.

regimes.name: Washington
regimes.detail: No single act, so five instruments: the My Health My Data Act for algorithmic health inference, HB 1170 provenance (2026 c 167, from 1 February 2027), HB 2225 companion chatbots (2026 c 168, from 1 January 2027), the prior-authorisation limits on AI-only denials in RCW 48.43.830 (in force since 11 June 2026), and RCW 43.105 for public agencies.

crossBorder.scopeBody: Each regime has its own deterministic rules module. It reads the jurisdictions your organisation has declared plus a handful of screening answers, and returns one of three states.

scopeStates.name: Applies
scopeStates.description: The regime reaches this system, and its overlay questions and requirements attach.

scopeStates.name: Does not apply
scopeStates.description: Someone answered the questions that rule it out. This is an assertion, so it is only ever made from answers a person actually gave.

scopeStates.name: Undetermined
scopeStates.description: Nobody has answered yet. Nothing attaches, and the state is shown as an open question rather than being read as a no. An unanswered question is a visible gap, never a silent one.

crossBorder.reuseBody: Where two regimes ask the same legal question, the product reuses the answer rather than asking twice. A California ADMT determination that finds the technology is the sole factor in a significant decision also answers the GDPR Article 22 question, and a positive determination with a named decision domain answers the Colorado covered-technology test. The assessment records which answer it inferred from, so the reasoning stays auditable.
crossBorder.artifactsBody: From one answered assessment the product assembles four documents. Assembly is deterministic: no model is called, so a document that cites statute is reproducible and every sentence traces to an answer. They download as Markdown so they can go straight into your own systems of record.

artifacts.name: Unified impact assessment
artifacts.description: One record answering the EU AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment, the GDPR data protection impact assessment, the California risk assessment and the state regimes.

artifacts.name: Multi-jurisdictional AI notice
artifacts.description: A universal core drafted to the strictest regime, plus one addendum for each jurisdiction that adds obligations of its own. The addenda never mix.

artifacts.name: Human review and appeal protocol
artifacts.description: One review workflow satisfying GDPR Article 22(3), the California human-appeal exception, the Colorado review right and the EU AI Act right to an explanation, with a table of what each jurisdiction words differently.

artifacts.name: Agentic addendum
artifacts.description: The stress test as a document: where each of the three breaks when the system hands off to an autonomous agent, and the provisions that layer demands.

crossBorder.gapsBody: An unanswered question does not silently drop the paragraph it would have filled. It becomes a visible gap carrying the obligation it would have evidenced, and every gap is collected into an open-items summary at the top of the document. A generated document that quietly omits an unanswered obligation is worse than no document, because it reads as complete.
crossBorder.agenticBody1: Every regime in this product was written for a system that produces an output which a person then uses. An autonomous agent that acts on that output breaks that assumption in a different place in each regime.
crossBorder.agenticBody2: The stress test runs eleven findings over the system, each naming the document it breaks, the assumption the regime made, what the handoff does to it, and the provision the agentic layer demands. Findings are gated on the regimes that actually apply, so a Texas deployer is not shown a GDPR failure.

agenticExamples.name: The Article 22 boundary moves to the agent
agenticExamples.description: Your analysis said the decision is not solely automated because a person reviews the output. If an agent then acts on it and nobody reviews the action, the decision the person experiences is solely automated after all.

agenticExamples.name: The human-involvement prongs fail at the handoff
agenticExamples.description: The California test requires a reviewer with authority to change the decision. An agent that executes before review completes removes that authority in practice, and the test is conjunctive.

agenticExamples.name: The protocol reviews what cannot be reversed
agenticExamples.description: With an agent in the chain the action is often complete before anyone appeals. Review without reversal is not the human intervention the GDPR requires.

startSteps.body: In Settings, record where the organisation operates. Nothing can resolve until this is done, and the product says so rather than guessing.

Five questions, each shown only if a jurisdiction you declared turns on it. Whether you are a public agency, a health carrier, a health care provider, a covered generative AI provider, or process Washington consumer health data.

startSteps.step: Open a system's Cross-border regimes tab
startSteps.body: See which regimes apply and which are still undetermined, then answer the system screening: how automated the decision is, whether special-category data is involved, and whether the output goes to an autonomous agent.

startSteps.step: Attach the requirements and create the assessment
startSteps.body: The in-scope requirements attach to the system's compliance record, and the unified assessment is created with the question set that system actually needs.
Download the assessment, the notice, the protocol and the agentic addendum. Answer more questions and regenerate: the gaps close as you go.

whatsNew.metaDescription: One assessment answering six regulatory regimes, three generated documents, an agentic stress test and the vendor supply chain.
whatsNew.title: What's new
whatsNew.intro: The releases below are listed newest first. Every regulatory addition carries a law-review date and a pending legal sign-off marker.

releases.headline: One assessment, five regimes
releases.summary: Most organisations deploying AI now answer to several regulators at once, and reconciling them by hand is where governance programmes stall. This release makes one impact assessment answer all of them, and generates the documents each regime expects.

items.title: Four more regulatory regimes
items.body: GDPR, Colorado SB 26-189, Texas TRAIGA and Washington's five domain instruments join the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001 and California ADMT. That is 294 requirements across eight frameworks and 115 cross-framework mappings, all bilingual. Each regime resolves its own scope from your declared jurisdictions and a few screening answers, and an unanswered question stays visibly undetermined rather than quietly reading as a no.

items.title: The unified impact assessment
items.body: One question set with a common core drafted to the strictest formulation among the regimes, plus overlays that appear only where a regime applies. Every question declares the requirement codes its answer evidences, so one answer stands as evidence in several compliance registers at once. Where two regimes ask the same legal question the product reuses the answer: a California ADMT sole-factor finding also answers the GDPR Article 22 question.

items.title: Three documents you can take away
items.body: The unified impact assessment, a multi-jurisdictional notice built as a universal core plus one addendum per jurisdiction, and a human review and appeal protocol with a table of what each jurisdiction words differently. Assembly is deterministic, so a document that cites statute is reproducible. They download as Markdown, to go straight into your own systems of record.

items.title: Gaps are shown, not hidden
items.body: An unanswered question becomes a visible gap carrying the obligation it would have evidenced, collected into an open-items summary at the top of every document. Citations are filtered to the regimes that actually apply, so a document never names a state you do not operate in.

items.title: The agentic stress test
items.body: Eleven findings covering where each document breaks when the system hands its output to an autonomous downstream agent: the Article 22 boundary moving to the agent, the California human-involvement prongs failing at the handoff, a notice that no longer describes the decision, a protocol that reviews what cannot be reversed, records that trace the output rather than the action, and an agent that reaches past the processing contract. Each names the assumption the regime made and the provision the agentic layer demands.

items.title: The vendor supply chain
items.body: The vendor catalog has carried structured subprocessor lists for 254 vendors, with 604 entries cross-linked to other catalog vendors. They are now rendered: a supply chain on each catalog entry with the reverse view of who depends on it, a supply-chain tab on each of your vendors marking the subprocessors you already govern, and a shared-subprocessors card showing the providers sitting beneath more than one of your vendors. The Annex IV draft receives the list too.

items.title: A self-hosting upgrade fix
items.body: The migrator's pre-baseline check had never fired, so installs created before the migrations baseline could not upgrade. Both faults are fixed and the upgrade path is now verified against the published image on every release.

releases.headline: California, jurisdictions and the obligation calendar
releases.summary: The releases that made the product multi-jurisdictional in the first place.

items.title: California CCPA ADMT
items.body: The fourth compliance framework: 92 requirements, the three-prong human-involvement determination, significant-decision domains, opt-out basis, designated reviewer and appeal route, and the risk-assessment deadlines.

items.title: Jurisdictions and the regulatory calendar
items.body: A jurisdiction model on the organisation and per system, driving a dated obligation timeline bound to your own inventory rather than a generic list of deadlines.

items.title: Article 50 transparency
items.body: Per-system transparency profiles, the four obligations, marking methods and generated transparency statements.

whatsNew.pendingBody: The GDPR, Colorado, Texas and Washington packs, the unified assessment and the agentic stress test were signed off on 8 September 2026. The two Washington items previously flagged as unconfirmed were verified against the session laws first: HB 1170 is chapter 167, Laws of 2026, effective 1 February 2027, and HB 2225 is chapter 168, effective 1 January 2027. The prior-authorisation limits are in force from 11 June 2026, not 2027, because the January 2027 date shown against RCW 48.43.830 belongs to a later section that reconciles two 2025 amendments rather than to the artificial-intelligence duties. The EU AI Act and California ADMT packs carry their own review dates and are still pending sign-off; any document citing them says so.

ui.advertisingExcluded: § 7001(ddd)(6) expressly excludes advertising to a consumer. However automated it is, targeting or recommending advertising is not a significant decision.
ui.article10LiveSince: The duty to complete a risk assessment before initiating any of these has been live since 1 January 2026. Merely selling or sharing personal information is a trigger.
ui.securityFraudNotAnException: There are exactly three opt-out exceptions. Security, fraud prevention and physical safety are not among them: they limit only what must be disclosed under § 7220(d) and § 7222(c), never whether the opt-out must be offered.
ui.humanAppealRequires: This exception holds only if a named reviewer considers information the consumer submits, knows how to interpret the output, and has authority to change the decision.
ui.twoPartTest: A two-part test: the technology must work for its intended purpose AND must not unlawfully discriminate. Evidencing one without the other leaves the exception unmet.
ui.processingInitiatedHelp: When the triggering processing began. Left blank, the § 7155(b) backfill deadline cannot be determined: it reaches processing that started before 1 January 2026.

screening.title: California CCPA screening
screening.description: Five answers that decide which California duties reach you. Anything you leave unanswered stays visibly unanswered: we never read silence as “no”.
screening.auditIntro: The next three decide the Article 9 cybersecurity audit under § 7120(b). Revenue band alone never puts you in scope: it only selects the phase-in tier once you already are.

coveredBusiness.label: Is the organisation a “business” under the CCPA?
coveredBusiness.help: Met by any one of: annual gross revenue above the CPI-adjusted threshold ($26,625,000 for 2025–2026); buying, selling or sharing the personal information of 100,000+ consumers or households; or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information. There is no small-business exemption, the thresholds are the carve-out.

sellShareRevenue50Plus.label: Does 50% or more of annual revenue come from selling or sharing personal information?
sellShareRevenue50Plus.help: On its own this puts the organisation into the Article 9 cybersecurity-audit regime.

revenueOverCcpaThreshold.label: Is annual gross revenue above the CPI-adjusted CCPA threshold?
revenueOverCcpaThreshold.help: $26,625,000 for 2025–2026. The next CPI adjustment is due 1 January 2027 and has not been published. Asked separately from the revenue band because the under-$50M band spans both sides of this figure.

largeProcessingVolume.label: Did you process the personal information of 250,000+ consumers or households, or the sensitive personal information of 50,000+ consumers, last calendar year?
largeProcessingVolume.help: Combined with the previous answer, this is the second route into the Article 9 audit duty.

revenueBand.label: Which revenue band applies, for the audit phase-in?
revenueBand.help: Selects the § 7121(a) deadline once you are in scope: over $100M reports by 1 April 2028, $50M–$100M by 1 April 2029, under $50M by 1 April 2030. Each tier measures a different revenue year.

regimes.title: Cross-border regimes
regimes.description: GDPR, Colorado, Texas and Washington alongside the EU AI Act and California. Each regime resolves its own scope from your declared jurisdictions and a few screening answers.
regimes.reviewMarkerNote: Regulatory content for these regimes was signed off on 8 September 2026. The EU AI Act and California packs remain pending.
regimes.orgDescription: Five facts about the organisation. Each is tri-state: not answered stays visibly unanswered and never reads as no.
regimes.systemDescription: What this system does, in the terms each regime tests. Answers here decide which overlay questions the unified assessment asks.
regimes.attachNothing: Nothing to attach yet: no regime has resolved into scope.
regimes.declareJurisdictionsFirst: Declare the organisation's operating jurisdictions in settings before any regime can resolve.

isPublicAgency.label: Is the organisation a public agency or governmental entity?
isPublicAgency.help: Texas TRAIGA adds disclosure and social-scoring duties for government; Washington RCW 43.105 governs agency use of automated decision systems.

isHealthCarrier.label: Is the organisation a health carrier making prior-authorisation decisions?
isHealthCarrier.help: Washington RCW 48.43.830 bars an AI tool from denying, delaying or modifying coverage on its own.

isHealthcareProvider.label: Is the organisation a health care service provider?
isHealthcareProvider.help: Texas TRAIGA requires telling the patient when AI is used in their care.

isCoveredGenAiProvider.label: Does the organisation provide a generative AI system with more than one million monthly users, publicly available in Washington?
isCoveredGenAiProvider.help: That is the covered-provider test in Washington HB 1170, which requires provenance data in generated media.

processesConsumerHealthData.label: Does the organisation process consumer health data of Washington consumers?
processesConsumerHealthData.help: The My Health My Data Act includes health inferred by algorithms from non-health information.

solelyAutomatedLegalEffect.label: Is this a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects?
solelyAutomatedLegalEffect.help: GDPR Art. 22. A reviewer who only confirms the output does not take the decision outside it.

processesSpecialCategoryData.label: Does the system process or infer special-category data?
processesSpecialCategoryData.help: Health, biometric, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, political, religious, trade-union, sex life or sexual orientation. Inferences count.

materiallyInfluencesConsequentialDecisio.label: Does the system materially influence a consequential decision about a consumer?
materiallyInfluencesConsequentialDecisio.help: Colorado SB 26-189: education, employment, housing, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, legal services or essential government services.

isCompanionChatbot.label: Is this an AI companion chatbot?
isCompanionChatbot.help: Washington HB 2225: adaptive, human-like responses capable of sustaining a relationship across sessions.

usedInPriorAuthorization.label: Is the system used in prior-authorisation determinations?
usedInPriorAuthorization.help: Washington RCW 48.43.830. The tool may approve; it may not deny.

interactsWithConsumers.label: Do consumers interact with this system directly?

handsOffToAutonomousAgent.label: Does this system hand its output to an autonomous agent that can act without a person?
handsOffToAutonomousAgent.help: This is what the agentic stress test examines. No statute keys off it yet, which is precisely the gap the agentic addendum documents.

unified.title: Unified impact assessment
unified.subtitle: One question set answering the EU AI Act, the GDPR, California ADMT, Colorado, Texas and Washington at once.
unified.counts: {total} questions: {core} in the common core, {overlay} added by the regimes that apply
unified.noOverlays: No regime overlay has resolved yet. The common core is still answerable, and the assessment will say which regimes remain undetermined.
unified.declareFirst: Declare the organisation's operating jurisdictions before generating a unified assessment: without them no overlay can be resolved.
unified.previewTitle: What this system will be asked
unified.artifactsDescription: Assembled from the registry and the latest assessment answers. Unanswered questions appear as visible gaps carrying the obligation they would have evidenced.
unified.noAssessmentYet: No assessment answers recorded yet. The documents will generate as a complete set of gaps.
unified.stressDescription: Where each document breaks when this system hands its output to an autonomous downstream agent.
unified.stressNotDeclared: Nobody has answered whether this system hands its output to an autonomous agent. Answer that in the system screening to run the stress test.

agent.title: Agent governance
agent.description: How much this system does on its own, what it may reach, who is accountable and who can stop it. Every regime in this product assumes a system that produces an output a person then uses; an agent that acts on that output changes what each one asks of you.
agent.autonomyLabel: How much does it do on its own?
agent.controlsNone: Nothing further is expected at this level.
agent.undetermined: Nobody has answered how autonomous this system is. Until someone does, the agentic analysis does not run and the generated documents say so.
agent.isAgentic: The agentic overlay applies to this system. The stress test runs, and the assessment asks the agentic questions.
agent.notAgentic: The agentic overlay does not apply: a person stands between this system and its effect.
agent.fieldActionScope: What may it do without a person?
agent.fieldActionScopeHelp: A bounded list of action categories, not a general objective. An unconstrained objective is the fact a regulator will read as intent.
agent.fieldDownstream: Which agents or systems receive its output?
agent.fieldDownstreamHelp: Anything that acts further on what this system produces.
agent.fieldTools: Tools and services it may call
agent.fieldToolsHelp: One per line. An agent reaches further than the system's own contract does, so this is the list that has to sit inside your processing agreement.
agent.fieldSponsor: Who is accountable for what it does?
agent.fieldSponsorHelp: A named role or person, not a team.
agent.fieldKillSwitch: Who can stop it, and how quickly?
agent.fieldKillSwitchHelp: Include what happens to actions already in flight.
agent.fieldKillSwitchTested: When was stopping it last exercised?
agent.fieldKillSwitchTestedHelp: A control that has never been used is a claim, not a control.
agent.fieldReversal: How long can an action still be reversed?
agent.fieldReversalHelp: Review without reversal is not the human intervention the GDPR requires.
agent.fieldTraceability: How is an action traced back to the decision?
agent.fieldTraceabilityHelp: The decision, the model version and the data behind it.

team.description: Who works on this organization's AI governance, and with which role. Owners, admins and AI officers can approve; members document; viewers read.
team.addHint: The person must have signed in to AI SENTINEL once with this email. Only owners can grant the owner role or change roles.

deleteOrganization.description: Permanently deletes {name} and everything in it: systems, assessments, policies, evidence, vendors and history. This cannot be undone. Export the program pack first if you need a record. Type the organization's name to confirm.

audit.title: Audit trail
audit.subtitle: Every recorded change, newest first: who did it, to what, and when. The trail is written by the actions themselves and cannot be edited here.
audit.restricted: The audit trail is available to owners, admins and AI officers.
audit.empty: Nothing recorded yet for this organization.
audit.exportHint: The export carries the generation time, the application version and the rule-pack versions in force, so the file can be placed in a production log.

assessmentVersions.intro: Each saved change, submission and decision is kept as a dated version, with a digest of its content. Versions are appended and cannot be edited or deleted.

assessmentVersions.noAnswers: No answers were recorded in this version.

sensitiveData.title: Sensitive data analysis
sensitiveData.subtitle: Decide, and record, whether a set of data should be treated as health data or another sensitive category.
sensitiveData.whyBody: US state laws define health data differently, and several of them turn on what the data is used for rather than what field it sits in. Five factors (source, content, use, consumer expectations, harm) give a repeatable way to reason, and the record of that reasoning is what a regulator asks to see.
sensitiveData.subjectPlaceholder: Audience segment, data feed, page group, field
sensitiveData.empty: No analyses yet. Start one for the first segment or feed you are unsure about.
sensitiveData.ruleSays: On these ratings the rule gives:
sensitiveData.reasoningPlaceholder: Why this rating? Name the facts, not the conclusion.
sensitiveData.departureLabel: Why this differs from the rule
sensitiveData.departurePlaceholder: A considered departure is fine; an unexplained one is not.
sensitiveData.decisionLabel: What we will do about it
sensitiveData.decisionPlaceholder: Suppress in opt-in states, seek consent, restrict the use, treat as sensitive everywhere.
sensitiveData.ownerPlaceholder: Who is answerable for this analysis
sensitiveData.nextReviewHint: Definitions, industry practice and expectations all move. Set a date rather than trusting memory.

dataFlow.rolesDescription: The data-protection role decides which duties attach; the transaction role is how your industry describes the same position. Retention is stated the way it appears in your notice and contracts.
dataFlow.inboundDescription: Each source, where it actually comes from, what sensitive categories it carries, and how long it is kept.
dataFlow.noSources: No data sources recorded yet. Add them on the data sources tab.
dataFlow.sensitiveHere: Sensitive categories present in this source
dataFlow.outboundDescription: Every recipient, what they receive, why, under which contract and for how long. An empty field here is the finding, so it is shown rather than hidden.
dataFlow.noRecipients: No recipients recorded. A system that discloses nothing is unusual; record that it discloses nothing rather than leaving it blank.
dataFlow.gaps: {contracts} recipient(s) with no contract recorded, {retention} with no retention.
dataFlow.sensitiveLeaves: Sensitive data reaches a recipient outside your control: {categories}. In most US states that is a sale or a share unless an exemption applies.
dataFlow.purposePlaceholder: Why they receive it, in your own words
dataFlow.sensitiveSent: Sensitive categories sent to this recipient

legalHold.title: Legal hold
legalHold.description: When litigation or an investigation is reasonably anticipated, nothing in scope may be deleted. A hold enforces that here, and stops the automatic pruning of program snapshots.
legalHold.noneActive: No hold is in force. Deletion follows the ordinary rules.
legalHold.matterPlaceholder: The name or reference counsel uses
legalHold.reasonPlaceholder: What is anticipated, and what must be preserved
legalHold.releaseReasonPlaceholder: Why the duty to preserve has ended
legalHold.effect: While a hold is in force, deleting systems, vendors, evidence, recipients, analyses, snapshots and the organization itself is refused.
